'The Ava-appointed governor at Pegu was assassinated on 29 November 1740' and the court chose a king on 8 December; Hanthawaddy controlled 'much of Lower Burma' by 1745, with Prome and Toungoo in Ava's hands until then ('Prome eventually fell to the Mons in 1745'). Martaban and Tavoy 'kept Siamese protection'. Cliopatria removes the Bago region (including Prome and Toungoo) in 1741.

correction.text: the same outline, for 1745-1751 only

keyframe_review.note: 352,471 km2 (1,249 cells), applied to 1745-1751: Bago region 92, Ayeyarwady 90, Kayin 88, Yangon 33, Mon 32 and Tanintharyi 15 are gone, which holds from the fall of Prome and Toungoo to the Mons ('Prome eventually fell to the Mons in 1745'; 'By 1745, Hanthawaddy controlled much of Lower Burma, and parts of Upper Burma up to Prome and Toungoo'). Cliopatria's Konbaung Dynasty row of 1741 (116,000 km2, 13.9-18.8 N) is this Mon kingdom's land.

correction.text: the 1751 outline: Toungoo's last realm, to 22 March 1752 only; from 1752 it is Mon (Ava and the south) and Konbaung (Upper Burma north of Ava)

keyframe_review.note: 334,303 km2 for 1752-1756. 'Ava fell to the Mons on 22 March 1752'; the last king was taken to Pegu and executed in 1754; Aung Zeya founded the Konbaung dynasty in March 1752 and 'had reconquered all of Upper Burma north of Ava' by December 1752, with Ava itself falling to him about December 1753 (Restored Hanthawaddy page). The shape is Toungoo's only until 22 March 1752; 1753-1756 is Konbaung and Mon land.

ledger.note: 1502: Mingyi Nyo's Toungoo, de facto independent of Ava since 1501, holds Kyaukse. 'Toungoo had been de facto independent since 1501' (Minkhaung II died in April 1501) and in 1502 Ava's new king gave Nyo the Kyaukse granary to keep him loyal; Nyo 'formally announced Toungoo's independence' on 16 October 1510 and was crowned on 11 April 1511 (Mingyi Nyo page). The First Toungoo Empire page has 'By 1502, Mingyi Nyo had already decided to break away'; 1502 is also Cliopatria's first shape and the year of the ava-kingdom loss.

Late 1538: Toungoo takes Pegu. 'Toungoo forces took Pegu without firing a shot in late 1538 or early 1539' (First Toungoo page: 'They finally broke through in 1538, capturing Pegu (Bago)', after annual raids from 1534).
1539: Tabinshwehti moves the capital from Toungoo to Pegu ('In 1539, Tabinshwehti moved the capital to Pegu'; infobox 'Pegu (Bago) (1539-1599)').

1539: the Irrawaddy delta. After Pegu fell without a fight in late 1538 and Bayinnaung beat the Hanthawaddy army at Naungyo (undated), Toungoo 'now held two out of the three Hanthawaddy provinces (the Irrawaddy delta and Pegu)' (Toungoo-Hanthawaddy War page); the page gives no month or year for the delta itself, so 1539 follows the hanthawaddy-kingdom dossier (1538-39) and Cliopatria's 1540 shape, which holds 83 Ayeyarwady cells.
November 1540: a Toungoo force attacks Martaban. 'In November 1540, 13,000-strong Toungoo land and naval forces attacked the city' (Toungoo-Hanthawaddy War page); the siege lasts seven months.
Late 1541: Toungoo besieges Prome, which had sheltered fleeing Hanthawaddy troops in 1539. 'In late 1541, Toungoo again laid siege to Prome.'

region.text: the Martaban province: Martaban, Moulmein and the south

ledger.note: May 1541: Martaban falls and the Mon south submits. The city fell 'right before the rainy season in May 1541'; 'The governors of Moulmein (Mawlamyaing) and southern territories' submitted. By 1541 Tabinshwehti 'had conquered the wealthier but disunited kingdom'.

May 1541: Martaban falls. 'In May 1541, seven months into the siege, Smim Payu launched the second attack on the harbor' and Toungoo took the city (Toungoo-Hanthawaddy War page); the gain of the Mon provinces follows.
19 May 1542: Prome surrenders. 'On 19 May 1542 (5th waxing of Nayon 904 ME), Minkhaung surrendered.'

19 May 1542: Toungoo annexes Prome. 'the small kingdom fell to the Toungoo (Taungoo) forces in 1542' (Tabinshwehti page: 'its king Minkhaung surrendered on 19 May 1542'). The shan-states dossier holds the same land as Confederation territory from 1533 and carries its own loss of 1542.

region.text: the Confederation's land from the Pagan country (Magway), the Mu and Chindwin edge

ledger.note: 1544: Tabinshwehti takes Pagan and is crowned there. He 'extended his rule to the ancient capital' in 1544 and 'made a triumphant return to Pegu in July/August 1544' (Toungoo dynasty page: 'In 1544, Tabinshwehti was crowned as king of all Burma at the ancient capital of Bagan'; First Toungoo page: 'from the Confederation by 1545', the year the shan-states dossier uses). The land is the Confederation's Pagan country as Cliopatria's 1547 shape shows it.

region.text: the Arakan coast from the Thandwe country to the environs of Launggyet

ledger.note: 28 October 1546: Toungoo invades Arakan. The invasion began 'on 28 October 1546' and reached 'the environs of Launggyet' on 23 January 1547; the kingdom-of-mrauk-u dossier has Toungoo hold Thandwe (Sandoway).

region.text: Ye and Tavoy on the Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: Late 1547: Saw Lagun Ein is sent against the Siamese at Ye and Tavoy. He was sent 'to drive out the Siamese forces from Ye and Tavoy in late 1547'; the page does not say they were driven out.

30 January 1547: truce with Min Bin. Tabinshwehti 'agreed to a truce with Min Bin on 30 January 1547'; the page records no conquest of Arakan and Cliopatria's 158-cell Arakan strip in the 1547 shape is unsupported.

region.text: Ye and Tavoy on the Tenasserim coast

ledger.note: February 1549: the Burmese retreat from Siam. The invasion came 'near the end of the rainy season on 14 October 1548'; the Siamese 'broke the siege in January 1549' and the Burmese 'negotiated a safe retreat in exchange for the nobles in February 1549'.

region.text: the provinces of the governors who declared themselves independent

ledger.note: 30 April 1550: Tabinshwehti is assassinated and his governors rebel. 'After Tabinshwehti's death, the empire he had built up in the last 15 years promptly fell apart.' Each major governor 'declared himself independent'; Smim Htaw had already raised a rebellion near Yangon in early 1550.

ledger.counterpart: Prome revolt of Thado Dhamma Yaza I
ledger.note: May 1550: Prome revolts. 'Thado Dhamma Yaza I revolted in May 1550 after Tabinshwehti's death.'

ledger.counterpart: Prome revolt of Thado Dhamma Yaza I
ledger.note: August 1551: Bayinnaung crushes the Prome revolt. The revolt 'was put down in August 1551 by Bayinnaung'.
1552: the empire is whole again. Bayinnaung needed 'to reunify the kingdom in the next two years' after 1550, and Cliopatria's 1552 shape has the empire without the Arakan strip.

region.text: Ava and Upper Burma, under the Confederation since 1527

ledger.note: 22 January 1555: Bayinnaung takes Ava and Upper Burma. 'The capital Ava fell to the southern forces on 22 January 1555'; Thado Minsaw was made viceroy on 19 February 1555.

region.text: the Shan plateau and the Kachin country

ledger.note: January 1557: Bayinnaung invades the Shan country. 'The invasion of the Shan country began in January 1557'; Thibaw, Momeik and Mogok fell on 25 January.

region.text: the northern Shan states and the Mohnyin-Mogaung country

ledger.note: March 1557: the cis-Salween Shan states fall. 'By March 1557, Bayinnaung in one stroke controlled most of the cis-Salween Shan states'; Mohnyin fell on 6 March and Mogaung on 11 March.

region.text: the Shan plateau and the Kachin country

ledger.note: March 1557: the fighting in the Shan country ends with most of the cis-Salween states in Toungoo hands.
November 1557: Mone, Nyaungshwe and Mobye fall. The last of the cis-Salween states named on the page submit in November 1557.

2 April 1558: Chiang Mai submits and Lan Na becomes a tributary. 'Mekuti surrendered without a fight on 2 April 1558' (infobox: 'Suzerain of Lan Na from 2 April 1558'); the Lan Na page has the kingdom 'a vassal state of the Toungoo dynasty in 1558' and 'Tributary of Burma (1st): 1558-1596'. After Mekuti's capture on 25 November 1564 a Burmese-appointed queen and then a prince-viceroy (January 1579) ruled it as a tributary. The tributary relation continues under the successor's slug lan-na from November 1564 (lan-na-kingdom dissolves then; see the vassal_end and vassal_start of 1564-11).

February 1560: Manipur submits. 'On 2 December 1559, he ordered an invasion of Manipur'; 'The Manipuri raja surrendered around February 1560' (First Toungoo page: Manipur 1560). Cliopatria draws the 81 Manipur cells inside the empire from 1564.
16 December 1562: Kengtung submits. 'The southernmost trans-Salween state of Kengtung submitted prior to the invasion on 16 December 1562.'

region.text: the Chinese Shan states on the Taping and Salween: Mong Mao, Theinni and the smaller states

ledger.note: March-April 1563: the Chinese Shan states of the Taping valley. The Taping valley invasion took place in March and April 1563 and Bayinnaung 'later held at least nominal suzerainty over the Chinese Shan states' (Theinni and the smaller states had sent tribute in 1558-59). Cliopatria draws 279 Yunnan cells inside the empire from 1564.

region.text: Kamphaeng Phet and the Northern Cities

ledger.note: December 1563: Toungoo's armies take Kamphaeng Phet. 'On 1 November 1563, five armies' left Pegu; 'The armies took the key central town of Kamphaeng Phet on 4 December 1563.'

union.text: the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet)

region.text: Kamphaeng Phet, the Northern Cities and Ayutthaya

ledger.note: 18 February 1564: Ayutthaya surrenders. 'The Siamese king surrendered on 18 February 1564.'

region.text: Siam's western strip: Tenasserim and the Mon uplands

ledger.note: 18 February 1564: Siam's western strip passes to Toungoo. The page dates only the surrender and a garrison at Tavoy from 17 June 1562; the strip (Tenasserim, the Mon uplands, 48 cells in Cliopatria's 1564 shape) is the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier's reading of the surrender.

region.text: Siam: the Ayutthaya kingdom's outline of 1588

ledger.note: 18 February 1564: Mahinthrathirat is installed as Siam's vassal king. 'The Siamese king surrendered on 18 February 1564'; infobox 'Suzerain of Siam from 18 February 1564'.

25 November 1564: Chiang Mai falls again and Lan Na passes to a Burmese-appointed ruler. Mekuti revolted during the 1563 Siam campaign; after Bayinnaung's new invasion of 23 October 1564 'Chiang Mai's defenders fled the city' on 25 November 1564, Mekuti submitted and was spared and sent to Pegu, and Queen Visuddhadevi was installed as vassal ruler (Bayinnaung page). The lan-na-kingdom dossier ends here (dissolve 1564-11, successor lan-na); the tributary relation goes on under the successor's slug.

November 1564: the same tributary state continues as lan-na. 'Tributary of Burma (1st): 1558-1596' is one unbroken span on the Lan Na page infobox; the slug changes because Cliopatria's Lan Na Kingdom shapes end in 1563 and its Lan Na row begins in 1600 (both share Wikidata Q1059707).
2 January 1565: Burmese armies take Vientiane. Bayinnaung's armies 'easily captured Vientiane on 2 January 1565' (infobox: 'Suzerain of Lan Xang from 2 January 1565, with later gaps').
1 August 1565: the Burmese leave Vientiane. 'The armies left Vientiane on 1 August 1565, after failing to catch King Setthathirath.'

region.text: Siam: the Ayutthaya kingdom's outline of 1588

ledger.note: 1568: Siam revolts. 'in 1568, Siam, the most powerful vassal state, revolted' (Bayinnaung 'learned on 12 May 1568 that southern Siam (Ayutthaya) too had revolted').

region.text: the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet)

ledger.note: 1568: war with Siam. Siam revolted in 1568; the Burmese counter-invasion followed.

union.text: the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet)

ledger.note: 2 August 1569: Ayutthaya falls again. Setthathirath was defeated on 8 May 1569 and 'The city fell on that very night on 2 August 1569.'

region.text: Siam: the Ayutthaya kingdom's outline of 1588

ledger.note: September 1569: Maha Thammarachathirat is made Siam's vassal king. The text has him appointed on 29 September 1569, the infobox table on 26 September 1569.

February 1570: Burmese troops hold Vientiane after Setthathirath leaves it. Bayinnaung 'personally led the two-pronged invasion of Lan Xang in October 1569'; Setthathirath 'made a stand at Vientiane for a few months before retreating into the jungle in February 1570' (Bayinnaung page, which does not say outright that the city was taken; the lan-xang dossier books the same occupation).
April 1570: Bayinnaung gives up. 'Bayinnaung finally called off the search in April 1570, and returned home' (Bayinnaung page).
July 1571: Mohnyin and Mogaung revolt. They 'collectively revolted in July 1571', refused conscription and revolted again in 1574; the Mohnyin saopha was killed in 1575.

December 1574: Lan Xang becomes a Burmese vassal kingdom, not an annexed province. The king's armies entered Vientiane without opposition on 6 December 1574 and Bayinnaung 'appointed a younger brother of Setthathirath, Maha Oupahat (Chao Tha Heua), king of Lan Xang' before returning to Pegu on 16 April 1575 (Bayinnaung page); the Lan Xang page calls 1574-1597 the 'Burmese Colonial Period' and has a Burmese vassal 'left to administer Vientiane'. The Bayinnaung infobox dates the suzerainty from 2 January 1565, when 'a son-in-law of Setthathirath' was installed as vassal king; that king did not last and the lan-xang dossier books 1565 as an occupation.
6 December 1574: Burmese armies enter Vientiane unopposed. 'On 6 December 1574, the king and his massive armies faced no opposition' (Bayinnaung page, as quoted in the lan-xang dossier).
16 April 1575: the Burmese king returns to Pegu. Bayinnaung 'returned to Pegu on 16 April 1575' after appointing Maha Oupahat king of Lan Xang (Bayinnaung page).
1576: Mohnyin and Mogaung are brought back. 'Hill states restored: Mohnyin and Mogaung in 1576'; the Mogaung saopha was brought before the king on 30 September 1577.
November 1580: the Burmese fleet occupies Sandoway. The king sent 'an 8000-strong naval invasion force on 15 October 1580' and 'The fleet occupied Sandoway in November 1580.'
1581: the invasion is called off. Reinforcements were sent on 28 August 1581, 'but the king died and the forces withdrew' (Bayinnaung died on 10 October 1581).

region.text: Siam: the Ayutthaya kingdom's outline of 1588

ledger.note: 1584: Siam is independent again. Nanda sent 'five major punitive campaigns against Siam between 1584 and 1593'; the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier has Naresuan proclaim independence in May 1584. The Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet, Phichit) lie inside the Siam outline: their rulers 'submitted, and were reappointed to their positions' in 1563-1564 (Bayinnaung page) and they return to Ayutthaya's direct rule in May 1584 (ayutthaya-kingdom dossier), so no loss of land is booked here.
December 1586: a Burmese army reaches Ayutthaya. Nanda Bayin's two-pronged invasion began on 19 October 1586 and 'reached Ayutthaya by December' (Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593) page).
20 April 1587: the Burmese withdraw after heavy losses, a Siamese victory (Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593) page).

1591: Lan Xang casts off Burmese allegiance. Nokeo Koumane 'declared Lan Xang independence and cast off any allegiance to the Toungoo Empire' and 'In 1591 he was crowned in Vientiane' (Lan Xang page). The Nanda Bayin page dates his revolt to about November 1595, has Lan Xang 'for all intents and purposes' independent by 1597 and the tributary ties officially renounced only in 1603; 1591 is kept for agreement with the lan-xang dossier (lan-xang_1588).

region.text: Suphan Buri and the road to Ayutthaya

ledger.note: Late December 1592: the Burmese reach Suphan Buri. A 24,000-man invasion began on 4 November 1592 and 'reached Suphan Buri after seven weeks' (Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593) page); the month is the page's start plus seven weeks.

1593: Manipur leaves the empire. The Nanda Bayin infobox lists 'Manipur (1581-93)' among the lands of his reign and the body text is silent; Cliopatria's 1588 shape already drops the Manipur cells (81 in 1564-1587), and the tint runs on to 1593 on this infobox (summariser's reading of the infobox).

Early 1593: Siam takes the Tenasserim coast. 'Early in 1593 King Naresuan sent two different forces to the cities of Tavoy and Tenasserim'; both fell after sieges of 15 and 20 days, 'agreed to remain subject' to Ayutthaya, and Mergui followed (Burmese-Siamese War (1593-1600) page); this matches the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier. The First Toungoo Empire page has 'Siam seized the entire Tenasserim coast in 1595' and the Nanda Bayin page 1594-95; the specific war page is followed.

region.text: Suphan Buri and the road to Ayutthaya

ledger.note: January 1593: the Burmese retreat with heavy casualties after the single combat at Nong Sarai (8 January 1593 in Burmese chronicles, 18 January in Siamese ones; Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593) page).

region.text: Moulmein, Martaban and the Mon provinces

ledger.note: 1594: the Mon provinces go to Siam. Siamese forces came to the aid of Moulmein's governor (his revolt is October 1594 on the Nanda Bayin page), 'the small Burmese garrison at Martaban abandoned the town', a relief force from Toungoo was beaten by a combined Siamese and Mon army, and 'The Mon provinces then became subject to Siam' (Burmese-Siamese War (1593-1600) page); the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier has 1594. Cliopatria drops them in 1595.

1596: Lan Na leaves. 'Lan Na's Nawrahta Minsaw declared independence in 1596'; 'all the vassals of Pegu went their own way by 1596-1597'. He became a vassal of Naresuan in 1602. This closes the span opened in 1558 (lan-na-kingdom) and continued as lan-na from November 1564; the Nanda Bayin page dates the revolt to late 1596 or early 1597 and the end of the suzerainty to about February 1597.
1597: the other vassals are gone. 'the rest of the vassals had broken away-de jure or de facto-by 1597'; Prome and Ava fought for central Burma in 1596-97.
1597: the Chinese Shan states are gone with the other vassals.

region.text: the Shan states and Kachin hills beyond Ava

ledger.counterpart: Shan states and other former vassals
ledger.note: 1597: the Shan states and the Kachin hills break away. Cliopatria's 1600 shape drops 191 Shan and 186 Kachin cells from the 1595 outline.

intersect.text: Lower Burma: Bago, Yangon, Ayeyarwady, Mon, Kayin and Tanintharyi

region.text: Lower Burma: Pegu, the delta, Martaban and the south

ledger.counterpart: Lower Burma lords: Toungoo, Prome, Syriam and Arakan
ledger.note: 1599: Lower Burma is lost to rival lords. Toungoo and Arakan (the kingdom-of-mrauk-u dossier names them) 'jointly invaded Lower Burma in 1598, and captured Pegu in 1599', and the imperial capital was burned in 1600; the Portuguese garrison at Syriam switched from Arakan to Goa in 1603. Prome and Toungoo were separate principalities until 1608 and 1610.

19 December 1599: the First Toungoo Empire falls and the dynasty continues at Ava. Infobox 'Fall of Toungoo Empire: 19 December 1599'; the Taungoo rulers 'withdrew from southern Burma and founded a second dynasty at Ava' (Toungoo dynasty page, 1597-1752): same state and colour (rule 2).
1599: the seat is Ava. The Taungoo rulers 'withdrew from southern Burma and founded a second dynasty at Ava'; Pegu was captured in 1599 and burned in 1600.
1600: Siam invades Lower Burma. 'Siam invaded Lower Burma in 1600.'
1600: Naresuan gives up. The First Toungoo page has no end date for the Siamese campaign; the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier has him give up at Toungoo in May 1600.

July 1608: Anaukpetlun takes Prome. 'In 1608, he took Prome (modern Pyay), installing his brother Thalun as the King of Prome'; the Prome page: 're-annexed by King Anaukpetlun in July 1608' after the revolt of 1594-1608.

region.text: Toungoo and Kyaukse, the Toungoo core

ledger.note: 1610: Anaukpetlun takes Toungoo. 'In 1610 he took Taungoo from Natshinnaung and forced the king to swear loyalty.'

1613: Anaukpetlun takes Syriam. 'He was able to counter the Rakhine fleets and took the port of Syriam in 1613, though Nat Shin Naung had already died.' (First Toungoo page: 'Portuguese Syriam (1613)'.)

region.text: Martaban, Tavoy and the Mon provinces

ledger.note: 1613: Martaban and Tavoy. 'Ava conquered ... Siamese Martaban and Tavoy (1613)'; the Anaukpetlun page has the 1613-1614 attack on Dawei and Tenasserim 'repelled' and Siam keeping Chiang Mai in 1618, the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier has Tavoy lost in 1613 and the Mon provinces in 1618.
1613: Anaukpetlun attacks the Siamese. 'In 1613-1614, Anaukpetlun attacked Dawei, Tenasserim and Chiang Mai but was repelled.'

1614: Lan Na is Burmese again. 'Ava conquered ... Lan Na (1614)'; 'After 1614, vassal kings of Burmese descent ruled Lan Na for over one hundred years' and the Lan Na infobox has 'Tributary of Burma (2nd): 1615-1628'.
1617: Anaukpetlun makes Bago his capital and is crowned King of Bago that year.

region.text: Dawei, Tenasserim, Martaban and Chiang Mai

ledger.note: 1618: Burma and Siam agree. 'In 1618 Siam and Burma reached an agreement in which Burma would control Mottama and Thailand would control Chiang Mai.'
1628: Lan Na is independent again. Lan Na infobox: 'Independent state: 1628-1631'; Anaukpetlun was assassinated in 1628.
1631: Lan Na is Burma's tributary for the third time. Lan Na infobox: 'Tributary of Burma (3rd): 1631-1727'.
1634: Thalun moves the capital to Ava ('Thalun was compelled to relocate the capital to Ava in 1634').

region.text: the northern Shan states and the Kachin hills; without Kengtung

ledger.counterpart: northern Shan states and Kachin hills
ledger.note: 1653: the northern Shan states and the Kachin hills are inside Cliopatria's shape again. The pages opened do not date it ('By 1622, the kingdom covered Lower Burma, Upper Burma, Shan States and Lan Na'); the 406 cells (Shan 187, Kachin 185, Yunnan 24) appear in the 1653 shape. The Pindale Min page, re-read on 2026-10-19, is silent on the northern Shan states, Hsenwi and the Kachin hills and on any gain in 1653 (Yongli 'fled to Bhamo'; Burmese armies under Pye failed to claim Chiang Hung), so the event stays at confidence 1. Fix fx-09 (F226): Kengtung is left out (see keyframe 1653).

November 1663: Narai invades Burma. He 'launched a three-pronged invasion of Burma' aimed at Papun, Martaban and Tavoy, after taking Chiang Mai in February 1663 and leaving it 'later that year' for a rebellious populace.

May 1664: the Siamese withdraw. In Rajanubhab's account the siege of Bagan 'ended when supplies ran out' and they withdrew before the rains; the Tenasserim cities 'fell back almost immediately under Burmese rule'. 'Burmese defensive victory.'

1727: Chiang Mai revolts and Lan Na is lost. 'In 1727, Chiang Mai revolted because of high taxation'; 'The resistance forces drove back the Burmese army in 1727-1728 and 1731-1732, after which Chiang Mai and Ping valley became independent'; infobox 'Independent city-states: 1727-1763'.

region.text: the northern Shan states and the Kachin hills; without Kengtung

ledger.counterpart: northern Shan states and Kachin hills
ledger.note: About 1738: the northern Shan states and the Kachin hills leave Cliopatria's shape. Unverified: the page has Manipur plunder 'the northern Burmese provinces' 'Five years into his reign' and says nothing of Shan states or Kachin hills. Fix fx-09 (F226): Kengtung is left out (see keyframe 1653).

region.text: Lower Burma: the delta, Pegu, the Mon provinces and Tenasserim

ledger.note: 29 November 1740: Pegu rises and Lower Burma is lost. 'The Ava-appointed governor at Pegu was assassinated on 29 November 1740 by the local court', which chose a king on 8 December; the Mahadhammaraza Dipadi page: the governor 'rebelled and proclaimed himself the King of Pegu in 1740'. The region is the 1738 outline's Mon lands (Martaban and Tavoy 'kept Siamese protection').

region.text: Prome and Toungoo, the Bago region without Pegu

ledger.note: 1745: Prome and Toungoo fall to the Mons. 'Prome eventually fell to the Mons in 1745' and 'By 1745, Hanthawaddy controlled much of Lower Burma, and parts of Upper Burma up to Prome and Toungoo' (Restored Hanthawaddy page).

region.text: Upper Burma around Sagaing and Ava

ledger.note: November 1751: Pegu invades Upper Burma. In November 1751 Binnya Dala launched a full-scale invasion of Upper Burma after annual raids up the Irrawaddy as far as Ava from 1742.

region.text: Upper Burma around Sagaing and Ava

ledger.note: 22 March 1752: Ava falls. 'Ava fell to the Mons on 22 March 1752' (Restored Hanthawaddy page: 'finally sacked the capital city of Ava in March 1752'); the king was taken captive to Pegu.

region.text: Ava and the Toungoo realm of 1751

ledger.note: 22 March 1752: the Mons take Ava and Upper Burma. The last Toungoo king was executed in 1754 and his son fled in 1755 to Mengmao in China.

22 March 1752: the Toungoo dynasty ends at Ava. Reign of Mahadhammaraza Dipadi '14 November 1733 - 22 March 1752'; 'The Hanthawaddy armies captured Inwa in 1752 and ended the 266-year-old Toungoo dynasty' (Toungoo dynasty page). Upper Burma north of Ava passes to Aung Zeya's Konbaung by December 1752.

wars.name: Toungoo-Hanthawaddy War

zones.text: Pegu, the delta and the Martaban province

wars.outcome: Toungoo conquers Hanthawaddy: Pegu in late 1538 or early 1539, the delta by 1539, Martaban in May 1541; Prome falls on 19 May 1542.
wars.note: 'In late 1534 ... he attacked Hanthawaddy. By 1541 he had conquered the wealthier but disunited kingdom.' The ledger carries the three dated gains; the contest events cover only the Prome siege because the pages opened do not date a campaign that held ground before the capture of Pegu.

wars.name: Toungoo conquest of the Pagan country
wars.outcome: Tabinshwehti takes Pagan from the Confederation of Shan States and is crowned there in 1544.
wars.note: Dated 1544 here and 'by 1545' on the First Toungoo page.

wars.name: Toungoo invasion of Arakan

zones.text: Arakan from Thandwe to the environs of Launggyet

wars.outcome: The invasion of 28 October 1546 reached Launggyet in January 1547 and ended in a truce on 30 January 1547; no Arakanese land is annexed.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1547-1549)
wars.outcome: The Burmese invasion of Siam (14 October 1548) fails: the siege is broken in January 1549 and the Burmese retreat in February 1549 in exchange for captive nobles. No border changes.

wars.name: Rebellion of the governors after Tabinshwehti
wars.outcome: The empire falls apart on 30 April 1550; Prome revolts in May 1550 and is put down in August 1551; Bayinnaung reunifies the kingdom within two years.
wars.note: Smim Htaw's rebellion near Yangon and Smim Sawhtut's plot are on the Tabinshwehti page; the pages give no dated border for the rebel governors.

wars.name: Toungoo conquest of Ava and the Shan states

zones.text: Upper Burma, the Shan plateau and the Kachin country

wars.outcome: Ava falls on 22 January 1555; most of the cis-Salween Shan states are Toungoo's by March 1557 and Mone, Nyaungshwe and Mobye in November 1557.

wars.name: Toungoo conquest of Lan Na, Manipur and the trans-Salween Shan states

zones.text: Lan Na (Chiang Mai): Mekuti 'surrendered without a fight on 2 April 1558'
Manipur: the raja surrendered around February 1560
Kengtung: submitted on 16 December 1562, before the invasion
the Taping valley and the Chinese Shan states: four 12,000-strong armies, March-April 1563

wars.outcome: Lan Na submits on 2 April 1558, Manipur around February 1560, Kengtung before 16 December 1562, the Taping valley in March-April 1563: all tributaries.
wars.note: No ground changed hands by battle: Mekuti 'surrendered without a fight', Manipur 'with minimal resistance', Kengtung 'submitted prior to the invasion', and the four armies in the Taping valley 'faced minimal resistance, and secured the allegiance of the local saophas' (Bayinnaung page, re-read 2026-10-19). Only vassal_start events are booked (ledger 1558-1563), no contest events; the zones are the four submitted lands, drawn as tints.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1563-1564)

zones.text: the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet)

wars.outcome: Five armies leave Pegu on 1 November 1563, take Kamphaeng Phet on 4 December and Ayutthaya surrenders on 18 February 1564; Mahinthrathirat becomes the vassal king.

wars.name: Burmese-Lao War (1565-1575)
wars.outcome: Vientiane taken on 2 January 1565 and left on 1 August 1565; Burmese troops hold it again from February to April 1570; entered unopposed on 6 December 1574, Maha Oupahat made king of a vassal Lan Xang and the Burmese king back at Pegu on 16 April 1575.
wars.note: October 1569: Bayinnaung 'personally led the two-pronged invasion of Lan Xang'; Setthathirath 'made a stand at Vientiane for a few months before retreating into the jungle in February 1570'; the search was called off in April 1570 (Bayinnaung page, re-read 2026-10-19). Lan Xang stays a vassal kingdom, not an annexed province (ledger, December 1574).

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1568-1569)

union.text: the Northern Cities (Phitsanulok, Sukhothai, Kamphaeng Phet)

wars.outcome: Siam revolts in 1568; Ayutthaya falls on 2 August 1569 and Maha Thammarachathirat is made vassal king in September 1569.

wars.name: Mohnyin and Mogaung revolts
wars.outcome: The two hill states revolt in July 1571 and again in 1574; the Mohnyin saopha is killed in 1575 and Mogaung is restored in 1576 (the Mogaung saopha before the king on 30 September 1577).

wars.name: Toungoo invasion of Arakan (1580-1581)
wars.outcome: A Burmese fleet sails on 15 October 1580 and occupies Sandoway in November; the invasion is called off when Bayinnaung dies in October 1581.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese wars (1584-1593)

zones.text: Ayutthaya and Suphan Buri, where the invasions of 1586-1587 and 1592-1593 were stopped
the Tenasserim coast, taken by Siam in early 1593

wars.outcome: Five punitive Burmese campaigns fail: Siam is independent from 3 May 1584, the Burmese reach Ayutthaya (December 1586 to April 1587) and Suphan Buri (December 1592 to January 1593) and are driven back; Siam then takes the Tenasserim coast in early 1593 and the Mon provinces in 1594.
wars.note: Campaigns on the Burmese-Siamese War (1584-1593) page: 1584-85 (repelled near the Sittaung and on the Chao Phraya), 1586 (Mingyi Swa from Lan Na, March to June, failed at Lampang), 19 October 1586 to 20 April 1587, 24 November 1590 to March 1591 (Lampang), 4 November 1592 to January 1593 (Nong Sarai). Contest events book the two campaigns that reached central Siam; the Tenasserim and Mon fronts are loss events (1593, 1594). The First Toungoo page has 'five major punitive campaigns against Siam between 1584 and 1593'.

wars.name: Collapse of the Toungoo Empire
wars.outcome: Siam seizes the Tenasserim coast in 1595; the vassals break away by 1597; Prome and Toungoo jointly invade Lower Burma in 1598 and capture Pegu in 1599; the empire falls on 19 December 1599 and Siam invades Lower Burma in 1600.

wars.name: Nyaungyan and Anaukpetlun's reunification
wars.outcome: Prome retaken in 1608, Toungoo in 1610, Syriam in 1613, Martaban and Tavoy in 1613, Lan Na in 1614; the 1618 agreement leaves Mottama to Burma and Chiang Mai to Siam (Anaukpetlun page).
wars.note: The Anaukpetlun page has the 1613-1614 attack on Dawei, Tenasserim and Chiang Mai repelled; the First Toungoo page has Martaban, Tavoy and Lan Na conquered.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1662-1664)
wars.outcome: Burmese defensive victory: Siam takes Chiang Mai in February 1663 and gives it up later that year; the three-pronged invasion of November 1663 is withdrawn in May 1664.

wars.name: Chiang Mai revolt against Burma

zones.text: Chiang Mai and the Ping valley

wars.outcome: The Burmese army is driven back in 1727-1728 and 1731-1732; Chiang Mai and the Ping valley are independent until 1757.

wars.name: Mon revolt and the fall of Ava
wars.outcome: Pegu rises on 29 November 1740; the Mons hold Prome from 1745; Ava is sacked on 22 March 1752 and the Toungoo dynasty ends.

certainty.note: The pages give no treaty or survey frontier for any period. The 1618 Burma-Siam agreement names Mottama and Chiang Mai but no line, and Cliopatria's outlines are 16-km cells; the Lower Burma coast and the Irrawaddy valley are firmer than the Shan, Kachin and Tenasserim hills, and every vassal tint (Lan Na, Siam, Lan Xang, the Chinese Shan states) is soft.

notes:
Page budget: nine pages for 22 Cliopatria shapes (First Toungoo Empire, Bayinnaung, Tabinshwehti, Toungoo dynasty, Anaukpetlun, Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom, Burmese-Siamese War 1662-1664, Lan Na, Mahadhammaraza Dipadi) plus the Prome Kingdom page opened for prome-kingdom. WebFetch summaries were used throughout, so the quotes are the summariser's quotations of each page. None of the pages gives an area, so the infobox comparison could not be made for any shape.

One state or three? Cliopatria's single row 1502-1756 joins the First Toungoo Empire (to 19 December 1599, Pegu), the Nyaungyan or Restored Toungoo dynasty (Ava, 1597-1752) and four years of Konbaung land. I kept one dossier, with a rename event at 1599: the house, the Burmese core and the claim continue, and the brief's rule 2 calls a dynasty change on the same land a rename. If the gap-fillers prefer two states, the split is at 1599 and the Wikipedia articles are 'First Toungoo Empire' and 'Toungoo dynasty'. The end is 22 March 1752 (Ava sacked), not Cliopatria's 1756: 1752-1756 is Mon (Ava and the south) and Konbaung (Upper Burma north of Ava) land; Cliopatria's 'Konbaung Dynasty' row of 1741-1751 (13.9-18.8 N, 116,000 km2) appears to be the Mon Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom, which Cliopatria lacks (needs a dossier: restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom, 1740-1757).

Corrections to Cliopatria (new keyframes override its shapes in their years): 1539 (Pegu), 1541-1546 (Martaban, Prome, Pagan, instead of everything at 1547), the 1547 shape without 158 Arakan cells, 1555 (Ava), 1557 (the Shan and Kachin country, instead of 1564), 1564-1599 and 1619-1726 without the tributaries that the vassal events draw as tints (Lan Na, the Chinese Shan states, Kengtung, Manipur; from 1572 also Siam and Lan Xang, which ayutthaya-kingdom and lan-xang draw as their own), new 1593 and 1594 shapes for the Tenasserim coast and the Mon provinces, 1595 with Pegu kept, 1600-1612 as Upper Burma only (Prome 1608, Toungoo 1610, Syriam, Martaban and Tavoy 1613), 1662-1669 with the Mon strip, 1727 (Lan Na out), 1740 (Mon Lower Burma out, Prome and Toungoo kept to 1745).

Disagreements between pages: the Pagan conquest 1544 (Tabinshwehti, Toungoo dynasty) against 'by 1545' (First Toungoo; the shan-states dossier uses 1545); the 1613-1614 Chiang Mai and Dawei attacks 'repelled' with Chiang Mai Siamese in 1618 (Anaukpetlun) against Lan Na conquered in 1614 (First Toungoo) and a Burmese tributary from 1615 (Lan Na); the Tenasserim coast seized by Siam in 1595 (First Toungoo) against 1593 (ayutthaya-kingdom dossier); Siamese vassal king appointed 29 September 1569 (Bayinnaung text) or 26 September (infobox); the end of the dynasty 1752 (this page) against Hanthawaddy's 'March 1752' and the 23 April 1752 some sources give (not on any page opened).

Events that rest on silence (confidence 1): the northern Shan and Kachin cells' return (1653) and loss (1738), both on Cliopatria alone; the Pindale Min, Mahadhammaraza Dipadi and Restored Toungoo dynasty pages do not date them. Raised in the repair run: the 1502 founding (Mingyi Nyo page: de facto independent since 1501, Kyaukse in 1502, formal independence 16 October 1510), the delta of 1539 (Toungoo-Hanthawaddy War page), Lan Xang's vassalage from December 1574 and its end in 1591 (Bayinnaung and Lan Xang pages), the Manipur exit in 1593 (Nanda Bayin infobox) and the Siamese seizure of the Tenasserim coast (early 1593) and the Mon provinces (1594) from the Burmese-Siamese War (1593-1600) page, so the first run's 1595 and the ayutthaya-kingdom dossier now agree.

Not drawn: the Yamethin and Taungdwin raids of 1523-1526; Mergui 'annexed at least by 1568' (First Toungoo footnote); Ceylon and the Tooth relic; the Mong Mao and Ming frontier (a ming-dynasty matter); the Meitei raids of the 1720s-1730s (no territory); Siamese occupation of Chiang Mai in February 1663 (owned by ayutthaya-kingdom, counterpart lan-na); Bengal. The ruler strip is the List of Burmese monarchs table (repair run), reigns from 1510 with Mingyi Nyo's de facto rule since 1501-1502 added.

Counterparts without a dossier: restored-hanthawaddy-kingdom (1740-1757), Manipur Kingdom, Kengtung, the Chinese Shan states (Mong Mao and the Taping valley), Mohnyin and Mogaung, Portuguese Syriam (Filipe de Brito, 1599-1613), Natshinnaung's Toungoo and the Prome principality 1594-1608. Gazetteer names used by coordinates: Ye, Kengtung, Syriam (Thanlyin), Pegu, Sandoway (Thandwe).

Repair run (2026-10-19), after the adversarial review. One vassal rule now holds for the whole dossier: tributaries are drawn by the vassal events, never inside the outline. Subtracted from the Cliopatria shapes of their spans: Lan Na (180 cells; tributary 1558-1596, 1615-1628, 1631-1727, independent 1628-1631), the Chinese Shan states (279 Yunnan cells, 1563-1597), Kengtung (87, 1562-1597, also taken out of the 1557 shape), Manipur (81, 1560-1593) and, from 1572, Siam and Lan Xang (the latter's 1,310 cells in 1579-1587 no longer double-claimed with lan-xang_1575 and _1579). The 111 Nagaland, Mizoram, Assam and Arunachal cells of the 1564-1587 shapes are removed too: the Bayinnaung page, re-read, names none of those lands and the ledger books no gain there (Cliopatria may rest on a source not opened; restore them if a page is found). Ledger: the December 1574 'gain' of Vientiane is now a vassal_start for Lan Xang plus an occupation pair 1574-12/1575-04 (the page has a vassal king appointed, not annexation), the confidence-1 1579 vassal_start is deleted, the May 1584 'loss' of the Northern Cities is deleted (never gained or drawn; they are inside the Siam outline, whose rulers 'submitted, and were reappointed'), the Martaban contest pair 1540-11/1541-05 and the Vientiane occupation pair 1570-02/04 are added, the Lan Na span is carried across the 1564-11 handover (lan-na-kingdom to lan-na), and four contest events for the invasions that reached Ayutthaya (December 1586 to April 1587) and Suphan Buri (December 1592 to January 1593) are added to the 1584-1593 war. The war of 1558-1563 now has its four zones and a note that only submissions are booked. Disagreements kept open: Lan Xang's break with Burma is 1591 (Lan Xang page, kept for the lan-xang dossier) against about November 1595 and 1597 (Nanda Bayin page); the Tenasserim coast is 1593 and the Mon provinces 1594 (Burmese-Siamese War (1593-1600) page) against 1595 (First Toungoo Empire page) and 1594-95 (Nanda Bayin); the Burmese-Lao War (1565-1575) article that the review suggested does not exist on Wikipedia (two URLs returned URL_NOT_FOUND; the Bayinnaung, Lan Xang and Setthathirath pages were used). Residuals not touched: the 1597 loss of the Shan states and the Kachin hills and the 1599 loss of Lower Burma are not cut out of the 1595 shape before 1600; the 1595-1600 Siamese contest at Pegu (ayutthaya-kingdom books it from January 1595) is only the 1600 pair here; ayutthaya-kingdom lacks the mirror contest pairs for 1586-1587 and 1592-1593 and lan-xang the vassal_start/vassal_end first-toungoo-empire pair; 1-2 border cells of Manipur and Arunachal stay in the 1619-1738 shapes.
